description: Curated collection of 9 research sources informing the redesign of the agent-knowledgebase Claude Code plugin. Focus: fix broken embeddings/kb-tool methods and remove uv as a hard plugin-server runtime dependency.

items.title: The death of RAG has been greatly exaggerated — LightRAG + Graph RAG for Claude Code in 2026
items.summary: Argues that naive RAG (chunk + embed + cosine) is obsolete at 2026 scale, but RAG as a pattern is still cost-optimal beyond ~2000 pages / ~1M tokens. Recommends graph/hybrid/agentic RAG, concretely via LightRAG — a Dockerized open-source competitor to Microsoft GraphRAG that builds a parallel knowledge graph (entities + typed edges) alongside a vector store. Shows a clean Claude Code integration where each LightRAG REST endpoint becomes a skill. Relevant to the redesign because it identifies the exact failure mode of the current plugin's stack (chromadb + cosine only, no relationship layer) and offers a concrete drop-in upgrade path with Ollama-or-OpenAI embeddings. Also highlights that chunking strategy is the dominant source of silent retrieval failures — which matches reported failure symptoms in the current plugin.
key_claims: Naive chunk+embed+cosine RAG is insufficient; graph-enhanced RAG beats it on relationship queries at similar cost.
LightRAG is a Dockerized, production-usable Graph RAG implementation that supports both OpenAI and fully-local Ollama embeddings.
RAG is ~1250x cheaper than stuffing full context at ~2000+ page corpus sizes; break-even is real and matters for plugin scoping.
Each LightRAG REST endpoint maps cleanly to one Claude Code skill (query / upload / explore / status).
Chunking strategy (fixed vs semantic vs overlap) is the single largest source of silent retrieval failure in naive-RAG stacks.
Embedding-model choice must match between index and query — mixing remote and local models breaks retrieval silently.
design_implications: If keeping vector-based retrieval, add a graph layer (entities + typed edges) alongside the existing chromadb store, or scope explicitly to naive RAG and accept its limits.
Expose CRUD-shaped tools (upload / query / explore / status) as a first-class plugin surface in addition to low-level MCP methods.
Make the retrieval backend pluggable so chromadb, LightRAG, or a markdown-wiki mode are interchangeable behind one tool surface.
Enforce strict embedding-model identity between ingest and query paths (already partially done via dominant_embedding_model).
items.content:
KEY IDEA: Even with 1M+ context windows (Opus 4.6), RAG is still essential at 500–2000+ pages — cheaper and faster than agent-GP (grep-style) search. But NAIVE RAG is dead: pure Pinecone/Supabase 'chunk → embed → cosine' no longer cuts it. What works in 2026 is GRAPH RAG / HYBRID RAG / AGENTIC RAG.

HOW RAG BASELINE WORKS: (1) document → chunked; (2) each chunk → embedding model → vector in 1000s-dim space; (3) query → same embedding model → vector; (4) cosine similarity retrieves closest chunks; (5) augment prompt; (6) generate. This is naive RAG. It fails to capture relationships between concepts.

GRAPH RAG (LightRAG): Same chunking + vector store, BUT also build a knowledge graph in parallel — entities = nodes, relationships between entities = edges with text descriptions. Example: chunk 'Anthropic created Claude Code' becomes two entities (Anthropic, Claude Code) + one edge (created). Query retrieval does vector lookup AND traverses the knowledge graph, so you can ask 'how do theories X and Y relate' instead of just 'what says warships'.

LIGHTRAG: Open-source repo, competes with Microsoft GraphRAG at a small percentage of the cost. Dockerized (Docker Desktop + docker compose). Web UI at localhost:9621. Supports OpenAI text-embedding-3-large embeddings OR fully local Ollama. Exposes REST API — each endpoint becomes a Claude Code skill. Four main skills: query, upload, explore, status.

CLAUDE CODE INTEGRATION: Each LightRAG API endpoint → one skill file. Skills use a standard schema (description, parameters, call pattern). Claude Code summarizes the raw JSON response from LightRAG and cites references.

COST AT SCALE: Study showed RAG ~1250x cheaper than textual-LLM at large corpus sizes (Gemini 2.0, July 2025 — ratio has narrowed but RAG is still cheaper at 500+ page scale). Break-even point: ~2000 text pages / ~1M tokens worth of corpus.

DEPLOYMENT OPTIONS: Local (fully inside one Docker container with local storage), semi-local (Docker + remote embeddings), or cloud (Postgres-backed LightRAG on Neon / managed Postgres).

DIRECT IMPLICATIONS FOR agent-knowledgebase PLUGIN:
- Current naive-RAG chromadb-only stack is out of date; consider adding graph layer (entity + relationship extraction) OR admit naive-RAG scope and just make it work.
- Embedding model choice matters: text-embedding-3-large is the modern OpenAI default; local default all-MiniLM-L6-v2 is fine for semantic proximity but doesn't give dimension matching with remote models.
- Document chunking is the biggest source of silent retrieval failure. Consider fixed-size + overlap (already in config) but also consider semantic chunking.
- Consider offering a 'skill-based' CRUD interface (upload / query / explore / status) as a first-class plugin surface, in addition to raw MCP tools.

items.title: The 4 Design Patterns Behind Every AI Agent — Tool Use, RAG, Planning, Multi-Agent
items.summary: Frames Andrew Ng's four agent design patterns (tool use, RAG, planning, multi-agent) and argues RAG is only one of four and is inherently reactive. Important for the redesign because it clarifies the plugin's role: it should be a fast, stateless, structured-JSON RAG tool surface — not a mini-agent. Consumers (Claude Code, other agents) compose it with their own planning/tool-use/multi-agent loops. This directly constrains the API surface area and discourages ambient state, hidden planning, or chat history inside the plugin.
key_claims: Every real agent composes from four patterns: tool use, RAG, planning, multi-agent.
RAG is a reactive pattern — the agent only retrieves when asked; it does not decide what to retrieve on its own.
Tool use requires the LLM to emit structured JSON and a separate executor to run the tool — this is the safety boundary.
Multi-agent is just composition of the other three; a KB tool should assume it will be called by many different agent shapes.
Claude Code itself uses three of the four patterns; the plugin should play well inside that composition.
design_implications: Keep the plugin's MCP tool surface fast, stateless per-call, and return structured JSON — do not embed planning or chat history.
Resist turning the plugin into a mini-agent; consumer agents will orchestrate retrieval and generation.
Tool descriptions should be unambiguous JSON-schema-shaped so tool-using agents can reliably select them.
Design for composition with planning agents: include predictable cost/latency characteristics in tool descriptions.
items.content:
FOUR FUNDAMENTAL AI-AGENT DESIGN PATTERNS (Andrew Ng): (1) Tool use; (2) RAG; (3) Planning; (4) Multi-agent. Every real agent is some combination of these four.

PATTERN 1 — TOOL USE: LLM generates a structured request (JSON), calling code executes the tool and returns the result. LLM never runs the tool itself — that is the safety boundary. Claude Code file edits, ChatGPT browsing, Copilot running tests — all tool use. 87% of IT leaders rank tool interoperability as critical for AI adoption.

PATTERN 2 — RAG: Gives the agent memory. Three steps: retrieve (similarity search over chunks/vectors) → augment (inject into prompt) → generate (LLM reads context and answers). Claude Code reading CLAUDE.md = RAG. GitHub Copilot repo indexing = RAG. Key: RAG is a REACTIVE pattern — agent only responds when asked.

PATTERN 3 — PLANNING: Three phases — decompose (goal → steps), execute (run each step via tool use), reflect (check result, replan on failure). 'Add authentication to my app' → Claude Code identifies patterns, creates ~10 steps, executes and adjusts. Planning composes with tool use + RAG: can use RAG to gather context before planning, tool use to execute each step.

PATTERN 4 — MULTI-AGENT: Team of specialized agents (researcher, analyst, writer, manager) each with own tools, knowledge, role. Single agent hits context-window ceiling + bloated instructions + tool conflicts. Solution: split responsibilities like microservices. Multi-agent is really patterns 1–3 composed: each agent uses tool use, some use RAG, the manager uses planning.

WHICH PATTERN TO USE: External systems (APIs/DBs/files) → tool use. Knowledge not in training data (docs/code/data) → RAG. Multi-step tasks → planning. Too complex for one agent → multi-agent. You almost never use just one — Claude Code uses three (tool use + RAG + planning), Devin uses all four.

DIRECT IMPLICATIONS FOR agent-knowledgebase PLUGIN: The plugin exposes only RAG-style tools (kb_query, kb_search, kb_ingest_*). It should be designed so consuming agents compose it with their own planning / tool-use / multi-agent loops — i.e. the plugin's tool surface should be fast, stateless per-call, return structured JSON, and NOT try to be an agent itself. Consumer agents will orchestrate.

items.title: ReFrag (Meta Super Intelligence Labs) — Precomputed embeddings during inference, 31x faster TTFT
items.summary: Explains Meta's ReFrag, which reuses the retrieved chunk's embedding directly during LLM inference (31x faster TTFT, 7x throughput over LLaMA-2 7B) and an RL-trained policy picks which sub-chunks to selectively decompress. More importantly for the redesign, the talk establishes two production patterns the current plugin lacks: (1) multi-vector-per-object retrieval (title, body, summary, named-vectors, late-interaction) and (2) MMR / symbolic filters for result diversity, not just raw cosine top-K. FreshStack's 'nugget coverage' is a better quality metric than top-K similarity alone.
key_claims: Reusing retrieved chunk embeddings in decoder prefill gives 31x TTFT speedup and 7x throughput by collapsing O(N^2) attention over a shorter sequence.
Multi-vector-per-object storage (dense + sub-chunks + token-level for Colbert) is now the production vector-DB pattern.
MMR (Maximal Marginal Relevance) and metadata filters beat pure cosine top-K on nugget coverage.
Curriculum learning + encoder-decoder latent-space reconstruction are the critical training stages for ReFrag.
RL-based selective-expansion policies are not dramatically better than perplexity or random expansion — added complexity is often not worth it.
Chunk-level summaries ('knowledge nuggets') stored alongside chunks materially improve retrieval quality without ReFrag-level complexity.
design_implications: Allow N vectors per page (title + body + summary) in the plugin schema to enable multi-vector retrieval.
Add an MMR option to the query path that reranks a top-K-vector-multiplier candidate set for coverage.
Expose symbolic filters (metadata.tags, source_type, date_range) as first-class query parameters alongside vector search.
Store per-chunk LLM-generated summaries alongside the chunk text to feed diversity/rerank stages cheaply.
Do not pursue ReFrag-level decoder changes — outside the plugin's scope; the low-hanging wins are multi-vector and MMR.
items.content:
REFRAG (Representation for RAG): Instead of throwing away the retrieved chunk's vector after retrieval, use it directly in LLM inference. Gains: 31× faster TTFT, 3× iterative-token speed, 7× throughput over LLaMA-2 7B.

ARCHITECTURE: (1) Chunk vector DB into ~256-token chunks (standard). (2) Each 256-token chunk is further split into fine-grained sub-chunks (e.g. 16×16-token sub-chunks). (3) Each sub-chunk is compressed to ONE embedding vector. (4) An RL-trained policy network (GRPO+PPO) decides which sub-chunks to SELECTIVELY EXPAND back into full token vectors — the rest stay as single compressed vectors. (5) Query token vectors + expanded sub-chunks + compressed sub-chunks all feed into the decoder.

WHY SO MUCH FASTER: Prefill is O(N²) attention. Compressing 16K input tokens to ~1000 chunk embeddings → 256× fewer FLOPs in prefill, smaller KV cache, faster decode.

TRAINING: 4-stage pipeline — (a) reconstruction: freeze decoder, train encoder + projection layer to reconstruct context from chunk embeddings (aligns encoder's latent space with decoder's); (b) continual pre-training: unfreeze decoder, curriculum-learning next-paragraph prediction; (c) RL selective-expansion policy with GRPO+PPO using negative-perplexity reward; (d) end-to-end fine-tune on downstream QA/summarization.

ABLATIONS: Curriculum learning is CRITICAL. Reconstruction (encoder-decoder latent-space alignment) is CRITICAL. The RL selective-expansion policy is not dramatically better than perplexity-based or even random expansion — so the complexity may not always be worth it.

DIVERSITY IN SEARCH RESULTS is the other big theme: not just top-K similar results, but MMR (Maximal Marginal Relevance), vector clustering, symbolic filters (metadata), multi-collection retrieval (query spanning papers + blogs + code). FreshStack benchmark measures 'nugget coverage' — how many distinct knowledge units the retrieved set covers, not just relevance.

MULTI-VECTOR PATTERN: The vector-database usage pattern has evolved: (a) single collection, billions of vectors; (b) multi-tenant (million tenants per schema); (c) NEW: MANY vectors per object (one object → 1 dense vector + N sub-chunk vectors + 256 token vectors for Colbert late-interaction). Weaviate named-vectors, Colbert late-interaction, Matryoshka representations, rotational quantization all enable this.

DIRECT IMPLICATIONS FOR agent-knowledgebase PLUGIN:
- Current schema: one page → one chunk vector. Consider allowing N vectors per page (title vector + body vector + summary vector) to enable diversity filtering.
- Add MMR option to query: rerank top-K-vector-multiplier with MMR for coverage rather than only relevance.
- Symbolic filters (metadata.tags, metadata.source_type, metadata.date_range) + vector search = the production pattern.
- For long corpora, chunk-level summaries ('knowledge nuggets') stored alongside the chunk enables better retrieval quality without ReFrag-level training complexity.

items.title: Karpathy's LLM Wiki — Markdown-based knowledge base with LLM-maintained index, no vector DB required
items.summary: The most consequential source for the redesign. Karpathy's observation is that at the plugin's actual target scale (hundreds of articles / ~500K words, one user), a plain markdown wiki with an LLM-maintained index.md plus [[wikilinks]] outperforms vector DBs on retrieval quality because the LLM follows explicit relational links rather than fuzzy cosine similarity. The architecture is just a directory (raw/, wiki/index.md, wiki/hot.md, log.md, CLAUDE.md) read and written by Claude Code itself — no server, no embeddings, no Python. Directly addresses both redesign goals: retrieval quality fails today because naive-RAG-at-small-scale is the wrong tool; and dropping the vector/embedding stack eliminates most of the reason uv exists in the .mcp.json.
key_claims: At ~500K-word single-user scale, an LLM-maintained markdown wiki beats vector RAG on retrieval quality by following explicit [[links]] rather than cosine similarity.
The full system is: raw/ + wiki/index.md + wiki/hot.md + log.md + CLAUDE.md — zero servers, zero embeddings.
Ingest is an LLM task: read source, emit 5-25 wiki pages, update index and log. Takes ~10 min per article via Claude Code.
Query is Claude reading CLAUDE.md then index.md then following backlinks; one user reported 95% token reduction vs loading all files.
Periodic 'lint' by the LLM catches inconsistent data, dangling pages, and suggests new-article candidates.
Vector RAG remains the right answer for 1000+ docs, multi-tenant, or latency-sensitive lookup — not for personal KBs in Claude Code.
design_implications: Offer a first-class markdown-wiki mode where each KB is a directory of .md files with an LLM-maintained index.md — no embeddings, no vector store, no Python server at query time.
This mode directly removes uv as a required runtime: Claude Code reads the filesystem natively.
Retain the Python MCP server only as a thin batch-ingest / SQL-import / de-dup layer that populates the markdown wiki.
Expose tools for lint / index-rebuild / dead-link-check as first-class operations so the LLM can maintain the wiki over time.
The QueryOrchestrator abstraction should be extended so 'backend=markdown' is a peer of 'backend=chromadb'.
items.content:
CORE INSIGHT (Andrej Karpathy): 'I thought I had to reach for fancy RAG, but the LLM has been pretty good about auto-maintaining index files and brief summaries of all documents and it reads all the important related data fairly easily at this small scale.' — At 100s of articles / ~500K words, a plain markdown wiki with an LLM-maintained index outperforms a vector DB for retrieval QUALITY because the LLM follows EXPLICIT LINKS rather than COSINE SIMILARITY.

STRUCTURE: A single vault directory containing:
  raw/              — ingested source documents (PDFs, articles, transcripts)
  wiki/             — LLM-generated wiki pages, one per entity/concept
    index.md        — flat index of every wiki page, organized by category (tools, techniques, concepts, people, sources, comparisons)
    hot.md          — ~500-char 'hot cache' of most-recent context (skips wiki crawl when irrelevant)
    log.md          — operation history (what was ingested, when, by whom)
    <subdir>/       — optional category subdirs (concepts, entities, analysis, sources)
  CLAUDE.md         — project rules: when to read wiki, when to skip, how to write new pages, how to lint

INGEST FLOW: (1) Drop a source (PDF/article/transcript) into raw/. (2) Prompt: 'Ingest X into the wiki.' (3) LLM reads, identifies entities + concepts + relationships, writes 5–25 wiki pages each linking to related pages via [[wikilinks]]. (4) Updates index.md with new entries under appropriate category. (5) Appends log.md entry. Takes ~10 min per article, ~14 min for 36 YouTube transcripts.

QUERY FLOW: (1) User asks a question via Claude Code. (2) Claude reads CLAUDE.md (knows the project). (3) Claude reads index.md to find relevant pages. (4) Claude follows [[backlinks]] to related pages. (5) Answers with citations. ONE user reported 95% token-usage reduction vs. loading all context files directly.

VS. VECTOR-DB RAG: Wiki wins on relationship understanding (explicit links > cosine similarity), infrastructure (0 — just markdown files), cost (~0 except LLM tokens), maintenance (periodic 'lint'). Vector RAG wins on scale (millions of docs) and true semantic-similarity-without-explicit-link recall.

LINT: Karpathy runs periodic LLM 'health checks' over the wiki: find inconsistent data, impute missing data with web search, find interesting connections for new-article candidates, detect unreachable pages.

WHEN TO USE WIKI-STYLE VS. VECTOR RAG:
  Wiki-style — 100s of pages, ~500K–1M words, single domain, consumption via an LLM agent.
  Vector RAG — 1000+ docs, true 'semantic fuzzy match' required, multi-user/multi-tenant, latency-sensitive lookup.
  BOTH — when you want backup retrieval quality: wiki for relationship questions, vector for 'what's similar to X' questions.

CLAUDE CODE AS RUNTIME: The entire wiki is read/written by Claude Code reading the filesystem. No server, no embedding, no DB. Plays naturally with version control (git).

DIRECT IMPLICATIONS FOR agent-knowledgebase PLUGIN — this is the BIGGEST SIGNAL in the research:
- The CURRENT agent-knowledgebase plugin architecture (chromadb + sentence-transformers + SQLite per-KB) is MASSIVELY over-engineered for the small-scale personal-KB use case it actually serves.
- Simpler alternative: the plugin could ship a mode where each KB is a directory of markdown files + an LLM-maintained index.md. No embeddings. No vector store. Just file-reading tools.
- This directly solves BOTH problems in the requirement: (a) embeddings don't need to work because they're not needed; (b) no uv required because no Python runtime is needed at all — Claude Code itself reads the markdown files.
- If we keep Python MCP server mode (for batch ingest / de-dup / SQL-source import), it becomes a THIN layer that populates the markdown wiki rather than a heavy vector pipeline.

items.title: LangChain AI Engineer's Guide — fundamentals of chains, agents, RAG (large transcript summary)
items.summary: Establishes the mainstream retriever abstraction (invoke(query) -> List[Document]) and shows the modern splitter hierarchy (character -> recursive -> markdown-header -> semantic). Advanced retrievers (MultiQuery, SelfQuery, ParentDocument) and rerankers (Cohere, BGE-Reranker) are called out as the 2026 production pattern. For the redesign, the key takeaway is that the plugin's QueryOrchestrator should be a true abstraction boundary: backend swapping (chromadb / markdown-wiki / LightRAG) should not change the MCP tool surface. Also validates markdown-header splitting as the correct default for markdown sources.
key_claims: A uniform retriever interface (invoke(query) -> List[Document]) allows any backend to slot into a RAG pipeline.
Text-splitter hierarchy matters: recursive/char-aware for prose, markdown-header-aware for markdown, semantic for dense material.
Advanced retrievers (MultiQuery, SelfQuery, ParentDocument) materially improve recall over naive top-K.
Reranking top-K-multiplier with BGE-Reranker or Cohere Rerank is the 2026 standard RAG pattern.
LangGraph state-machine agents have replaced the old AgentExecutor for complex flows — state as first-class, nodes as functions.
design_implications: Refactor QueryOrchestrator into a strict retriever-interface boundary so chromadb / markdown / LightRAG backends are swappable without API changes.
Use MarkdownHeaderTextSplitter as the default for markdown source_type.
Add an optional rerank stage with BGE-Reranker-v2 (runs CPU-local, small footprint).
Consider exposing a SelfQuery-style metadata filter parser to turn natural language into symbolic filters for tags/date/source_type.
items.content:
Large (243KB) 4-chapter course on LangChain/LangGraph. Key concepts relevant to agent-knowledgebase redesign:
- LangChain Expression Language (LCEL) treats chains as composable pipelines: retriever | prompt | LLM | parser.
- Retrievers are a first-class abstraction in LangChain with a consistent interface (invoke(query) -> List[Document]); any backend (Chroma, FAISS, Pinecone, custom) slots in.
- Document schema: page_content + metadata dict. Used by retrievers, text splitters, vector stores.
- Text splitters hierarchy: CharacterTextSplitter (naive) → RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter (respects paragraph/sentence boundaries) → MarkdownHeaderTextSplitter (structure-aware) → SemanticChunker (embedding-based boundary detection).
- MultiQueryRetriever / SelfQueryRetriever / ParentDocumentRetriever — advanced retrieval patterns: MultiQuery paraphrases the query N times, SelfQuery extracts metadata filters from natural language, ParentDocument retrieves a small chunk but returns its parent document to the LLM.
- Reranking (Cohere Rerank, BGE-Reranker) applied to top-K-vector-multiplier is the 2026 standard pattern.
- LangGraph: state-machine agent framework — each node is a function, edges define transitions. Replaces AgentExecutor for complex agents.

DIRECT IMPLICATIONS FOR agent-knowledgebase PLUGIN:
- Retriever abstraction layer: current codebase has QueryOrchestrator — consider making it pluggable so the vector backend is swappable (chromadb → in-memory → LightRAG → markdown-wiki) WITHOUT changing the MCP tool surface.
- Adopt Markdown-header-aware splitter as default for markdown sources (one of the documented source_types).
- Add optional reranking pass (BGE-Reranker-v2 runs fully local and is small).

items.title: LangChain Master Class for beginners — building RAG chatbots and agents (large transcript summary)
items.summary: A beginner-level walkthrough that is useful for the redesign because it enumerates the classic failure modes the current plugin is likely hitting: chunk_size too small (loses context), too large (dilutes similarity), overlap=0 (missed boundary facts), and mixing embedding models (dimension or semantic-space mismatch). Validates the plugin's existing dominant_embedding_model tracking and argues it should be strictly enforced: if a KB was built with model A, you must either refuse or auto-reembed when model B is used — never mix. Also recommends keeping chat-history rewriting out of the plugin (client-side), preserving a stateless query API.
key_claims: Standard RAG pipeline is load -> split -> embed -> store -> retrieve -> generate; each stage has failure modes.
Conversational/history-aware retrieval belongs in the client, not the retrieval service — keep query APIs stateless.
Mixing embedding models across writes and queries is a classic silent-failure bug in naive RAG stacks.
Chunk size and overlap tuning dominates retrieval quality more than model selection at small scale.
Tool-calling agents use KB tools through simple search(query) interfaces — mirror this shape in the plugin.
design_implications: Strictly enforce dominant_embedding_model: either reject heterogeneous writes or auto-reembed; do not silently mix.
Keep the query MCP tool stateless; put history-aware query rewriting in the calling agent.
Expose chunk_size and chunk_overlap as per-KB config with sane defaults for prose vs code vs markdown.
Keep the primary search tool a simple 'search(query, k, filters)' shape so any tool-calling agent can adopt it.
items.content:
Large (233KB) master class on LangChain for beginners. Key patterns relevant to agent-knowledgebase:
- Standard RAG pipeline: (load) DocumentLoader → (split) TextSplitter → (embed) Embeddings → (store) VectorStore → (retrieve) Retriever → (generate) LLM-with-RetrievalQAChain.
- Conversational RAG adds a history-aware retriever: rewrite the current query using the chat history before embedding it, so pronoun-resolution works ('what about its author?' becomes 'who wrote X?').
- Tool-calling agents use tools like 'search_knowledgebase(query)' that the LLM invokes — same surface as the agent-knowledgebase MCP tools.
- Common mistakes: chunk_size too small (loses context) or too big (dilutes similarity); overlap=0 (missed boundary facts); reusing embeddings across different models (dimension or semantic-space mismatch — exactly the bug the current plugin's dominant_embedding_model field was added to prevent).

DIRECT IMPLICATIONS FOR agent-knowledgebase PLUGIN:
- Existing embedding_model tracking per page is correct. Enforce it strictly: if a KB has N pages embedded with model A and you try to add page with model B, the service should either refuse or auto-reembed — not mix.
- History-aware rewriting should happen client-side (in the agent calling the plugin), not inside the plugin. Keep the plugin's query API stateless.

items.title: Running Python MCP servers without uv: pip/venv, pipx, uvx, Docker, and PEP-723 script runners
items.summary: Enumerates seven concrete paths to remove uv as a hard dependency: plain pip+venv, pipx, uvx (not a real solution), Docker, PEP-723 inline deps, plugin-shipped venv bootstrapped on first run, and pre-built PyInstaller binaries. Recommends plugin-local stdlib venv auto-bootstrapped on first call as the cleanest primary path, with pipx and Docker as documented alternates. Crucially observes that the fastest way to remove uv is to first shrink the dependency surface area — i.e. if the plugin adopts the markdown-wiki architecture, chromadb/sentence-transformers/torch all disappear and stdlib venv becomes trivial.
key_claims: Pattern A — plugin-local stdlib venv + tiny bash/cmd wrapper bootstrapped on first run — is the best primary path to remove uv.
uvx still requires uv installed and is not a valid 'remove uv' solution.
pipx is a viable fallback but adds its own install prerequisite and is slower than uv.
Docker gives zero-Python-on-host but requires Docker Desktop on Windows and adds ~2s cold start plus a 200+ MB image.
PEP-723 inline-dep single-file scripts are not yet mainstream in 2026; document as future path only.
Reducing the dependency surface area (e.g. dropping chromadb/sentence-transformers) is a prerequisite to any clean stdlib-venv bootstrap.
design_implications: Replace the current .mcp.json uv command with a plugin-local wrapper script (bash + .cmd) at ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/bin/run-server that auto-creates .venv on first run using stdlib venv.
Document pipx and Docker as alternate install paths in the plugin README, but do not rely on either as default.
Before implementing the venv bootstrap, shrink dependencies aggressively — the markdown-wiki path reduces deps to pydantic, httpx, mcp.
If retaining vector features, replace sentence-transformers with fastembed (ONNX) to keep the venv bootstrap fast and small.
items.content:
PROBLEM: The agent-knowledgebase plugin currently ships with `command: "uv", args: ["run", "--directory", "${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}", "python", "-m", "agent_knowledgebase.server"]` in its .mcp.json. This requires every user to have uv installed. Requirement: remove uv as a hard dependency.

ALTERNATIVES SURVEYED:

1) PLAIN pip + venv (no uv). Setup steps: (a) `python -m venv .venv` in plugin root; (b) `.venv/Scripts/pip install -e .`; (c) .mcp.json invokes `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/.venv/Scripts/python.exe -m agent_knowledgebase.server` (Windows) or `.venv/bin/python` (Unix). PROS: zero extra tools, standard library only. CONS: (a) the user must run setup once manually; (b) no lock file by default (pip-compile optional); (c) cross-platform script paths in .mcp.json require branching.

2) pipx (install from GitHub or PyPI). Setup: `pipx install agent-knowledgebase` or `pipx install git+https://github.com/goosefly99/agent-knowledgebase-claude-plugin.git`. .mcp.json becomes: `command: "agent-knowledgebase-server"` (a console_scripts entry point). PROS: isolated env, one-command install, widely available (shipped with many distros' python-pipx packages). CONS: (a) user must install pipx — still a dependency; (b) updating the plugin requires `pipx upgrade`; (c) pipx is slower than uv to install.

3) uvx (no uv-run, just uvx) — 'uvx agent-knowledgebase-server' ephemerally resolves + executes. Same basic story as uv run but using the subcommand that mirrors pipx. Still requires uv. NOT a real solution for removing uv dependency.

4) DOCKER CONTAINER. Setup: (a) provide Dockerfile in plugin root; (b) publish image to Docker Hub / GHCR on each release; (c) .mcp.json: `command: "docker", args: ["run", "-i", "--rm", "-v", "${AGENT_KB_SAVES_DIR}:/data", "ghcr.io/goosefly99/agent-knowledgebase:0.7.0"]`. PROS: zero Python-on-host required, lockfile-equivalent via image pinning, clean reproducibility. CONS: (a) Docker on Windows requires Docker Desktop; (b) host-container filesystem permissions are a setup hurdle; (c) startup is slower (~2s cold) than native Python; (d) 200+ MB image.

5) PEP-723 INLINE-DEPS SCRIPT. Python 3.13+ supports inline dependency metadata in single-file scripts. Setup: the plugin's entry point is a single Python file with a leading comment block listing its dependencies; `python script.py` automatically installs and runs with any PEP-723-aware runner (uv supports this, and CPython 3.14+ has stdlib support via `pip run`). NOT YET MAINSTREAM in 2026 — skip as primary solution, note as future.

6) PRE-INSTALLED VIRTUAL ENV SHIPPED WITH PLUGIN. The plugin installer script creates .venv on first run (postinstall hook or SessionStart hook) using stdlib `venv` + pip. After install, .mcp.json invokes the venv's python directly. NO TOOLS required besides Python itself. PROS: (a) pure stdlib; (b) one-time cost; (c) zero user friction after first run. CONS: platform-specific script paths (Scripts/ vs bin/), duplicated install logic.

7) PRE-BUILT BINARY (PyInstaller / Nuitka / shiv). Setup: bundle the plugin + all dependencies into a single executable, ship per-platform binary as a GitHub release artifact; .mcp.json invokes the binary directly. PROS: zero Python-on-host required, fast startup, no dependency install. CONS: larger artifact, CI needed for every platform, awkward for development iterations.

RECOMMENDATION (research synthesis): Option 6 (stdlib venv + SessionStart hook OR documented one-time setup) is the cleanest path forward for a Claude Code plugin targeting individual developer machines. Option 2 (pipx) is a reasonable fallback for users already in the Python-CLI-tool ecosystem. Option 4 (Docker) is attractive for heavy dependencies (chromadb, sentence-transformers, tree-sitter) but adds a Docker Desktop requirement that may exceed the plugin's target user base.

MOST IMPORTANT INSIGHT: If the plugin adopts the Karpathy-style markdown wiki architecture (see yt-sboNwYmH3AY), MOST OF THE CURRENT PYTHON DEPENDENCIES VANISH (no chromadb, no sentence-transformers, no sqlparse/sqlalchemy for vector-store-driven code paths), which in turn makes Option 6 (stdlib venv auto-bootstrap) trivial — just pydantic, httpx, mcp. The fastest path to removing uv is to first reduce the dependency surface area.

items.title: Lightweight embedding alternatives to sentence-transformers in 2026
items.summary: Surveys lightweight local embedding options (fastembed/ONNX MiniLM at ~100 MB vs ~2 GB torch stack, EmbeddingGemma, BGE-small-en-v1.5, gte-multilingual) and remote-only options (Ollama/vLLM/LocalAI/OpenAI via the plugin's already-implemented OpenAI-compatible /embeddings client). Core argument: the plugin's 2 GB torch/sentence-transformers install is the single biggest obstacle to a clean uv-free bootstrap. Recommends fastembed (same MiniLM vectors, ONNX runtime) if local embeddings stay; recommends remote-only by default (often Ollama) to shrink the plugin from ~2 GB to ~20 MB; notes that a wiki-style mode removes embeddings entirely.
key_claims: sentence-transformers pulls ~2 GB torch+transformers+tokenizers and dominates the plugin's install footprint.
fastembed provides the same all-MiniLM-L6-v2 vectors via ONNX at ~100 MB — a ~20x install shrink.
BGE-small-en-v1.5 (33M params, 384-dim) often beats MiniLM on MTEB while remaining small.
EmbeddingGemma is designed for on-device retrieval and is a viable modern default.
The plugin already supports remote OpenAI-compatible /embeddings endpoints (Ollama, vLLM, LocalAI), so a remote-only default is a small refactor.
Remote-only default drops plugin install size from ~2 GB to ~20 MB, making stdlib-venv bootstrap essentially free.
design_implications: Drop sentence-transformers from default dependencies; switch local-embedding path to fastembed (ONNX MiniLM).
Make local embedding model optional; default the plugin to remote Ollama at http://localhost:11434/v1 for users who already run Ollama.
If the plugin adopts the wiki-style mode, delete the entire embeddings/vectorstore module rather than slim it.
Document the trade-off clearly: local (private, zero network) vs remote (fast, tiny install) and let users choose per-KB.
items.content:
CURRENT DEFAULT IN PLUGIN: `all-MiniLM-L6-v2` via sentence-transformers — 22M params, 384-dim, ~5-14k sentences/sec on CPU. Solid baseline but a large dependency.

WHY EMBEDDINGS DEPENDENCY IS HEAVY: sentence-transformers pulls in torch, transformers, tokenizers. On first install this is ~2 GB download. This contributes significantly to the plugin's install surface area.

ALTERNATIVES:

1) STAY WITH all-MiniLM-L6-v2 but use ONNX Runtime instead of torch. `fastembed` library from Qdrant provides sentence-transformers-compatible API but uses ONNX models — ~100 MB install vs. ~2 GB for torch. Same MiniLM model, same vectors.

2) EMBEDDINGGEMMA (Google, 2025) — lightweight, designed for on-device retrieval. Fast inference on mobile-class hardware.

3) BGE-SMALL-EN-V1.5 — 33M params, 384-dim, often outperforms MiniLM on MTEB. Ships as GGUF and ONNX.

4) gte-multilingual-base (Alibaba) — 305M params, multilingual. Overkill for English-only plugin.

5) REMOTE-ONLY (skip local embeddings). The v0.7.0 changelog shows the plugin already supports `provider=remote` talking to any OpenAI-compatible /embeddings endpoint (Ollama, vLLM, LocalAI, OpenAI). If the plugin stops shipping a local embedder entirely, the sentence-transformers dep drops.

RECOMMENDATION: If embeddings remain in scope after redesign:
- (a) Replace sentence-transformers with `fastembed` for a 20× smaller install footprint with identical vectors.
- (b) Make local embeddings OPTIONAL; default to remote Ollama (`http://localhost:11434/v1`). This pushes the heavy model off the plugin and onto the user's existing Ollama install, which many Claude Code users already have running.
- (c) If remote-only, install size of the plugin drops from ~2 GB to ~20 MB — dramatically easier to bootstrap without uv.

IF PLUGIN GOES WIKI-STYLE (per yt-sboNwYmH3AY): Embeddings become entirely unnecessary. Delete the whole embeddings/vectorstore module. Retrieval is file-read over markdown + LLM-guided link traversal.

items.title: Claude Code plugin MCP server config patterns — command, args, env, CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT
items.summary: Documents the Claude Code plugin .mcp.json contract (command / args / env / ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT} substitution / stdio-http-sse transports) and distills four working patterns from community plugins: plugin-local venv + wrapper (A), system Python + PYTHONPATH (B), pipx console-script (C), and Docker (D). Recommends Pattern A (cross-platform wrapper at ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/bin/run-server that bootstraps .venv on first call) as the current best fit for the plugin's maturity level.
key_claims: .mcp.json expands ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT} to the plugin install path at launch, enabling self-contained launchers.
Pattern A (plugin-local venv + tiny bash/.cmd wrapper at ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/bin/run-server) is the best-fit primary distribution path.
Pattern B (system python + PYTHONPATH) is simplest but pushes dependency install onto the user.
Pattern C (pipx console-script via [project.scripts]) is a clean option for users already in the Python-CLI ecosystem.
Pattern D (Docker) gives zero-Python-on-host but at the cost of Docker Desktop as a new hard dependency.
design_implications: Update .mcp.json to invoke ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/bin/run-server with no args; ship bash (run-server) and Windows (run-server.cmd) siblings.
The wrapper creates .venv using stdlib venv on first call if absent, pip-installs requirements, then exec's the server.
Add [project.scripts] agent-knowledgebase-server entry for users who prefer pipx install.
Provide Dockerfile and GHCR publish workflow as an alternate zero-Python install path for advanced users.
items.content:
CLAUDE CODE PLUGIN .mcp.json contract: (a) `command` is the executable; (b) `args` are positional args; (c) `env` is optional envvar dict; (d) `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}` is substituted with the plugin install path at launch time; (e) `type` defaults to stdio; (f) transport can be stdio/http/sse.

CURRENT PLUGIN CONFIG (.mcp.json):
```
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "agent-knowledgebase": {
      "command": "uv",
      "args": ["run", "--directory", "${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}", "python", "-m", "agent_knowledgebase.server"]
    }
  }
}
```

WORKING PATTERNS WITHOUT uv (distilled from community plugins):

PATTERN A — Plugin-local venv + platform-dispatching wrapper script:
```
{
  "command": "${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/bin/run-server",
  "args": []
}
```
Where `bin/run-server` is a tiny platform-specific shim (bash + .cmd) that activates the plugin's .venv and runs the server. Venv is bootstrapped on first call if absent.

PATTERN B — System Python + PYTHONPATH:
```
{
  "command": "python",
  "args": ["-m", "agent_knowledgebase.server"],
  "env": { "PYTHONPATH": "${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/src" }
}
```
Requires user to `pip install` the plugin's deps themselves. Simplest but highest friction.

PATTERN C — pipx console-script:
```
{
  "command": "agent-knowledgebase-server",
  "args": []
}
```
Plugin `pyproject.toml` defines `[project.scripts] agent-knowledgebase-server = "agent_knowledgebase.server:main"`. User runs `pipx install agent-knowledgebase-claude-plugin` once.

PATTERN D — Docker:
```
{
  "command": "docker",
  "args": ["run", "-i", "--rm", "-v", "${AGENT_KB_SAVES_DIR}:/data", "ghcr.io/goosefly99/agent-knowledgebase:0.8.0"]
}
```
Zero Python-on-host. Slowest cold start.

DIRECT IMPLICATIONS FOR agent-knowledgebase PLUGIN:
- PATTERN A (plugin-local venv + wrapper script) is the best fit for current maturity: no new user tooling, auto-bootstraps first run, cross-platform via two small scripts (bash + .cmd) that live in the plugin.
- Ship PATTERN B as the 'advanced / bring-your-own-env' alternative in documentation.
- PATTERN C (pipx) is documented as a 'if you already have pipx' alternative.
- Document PATTERN D (docker) as the 'zero-install' alternative for users uncomfortable with Python tooling.
